Random Walks

ProbabilityCountingSequences
Game: A walker moves one step to the right and one step up or down at a time. See how many different routes can take it from A to B. There is nothing to win — watch the paths appear.
How to play: Move the sliders to choose the start, the finish and the number of steps. Press One walk or Ten walks, and tick Show names to label the endpoints.

Look for the math

A random walk is a path made of random steps. Here every step goes one place right and either one up or one down. Somewhere among all those choices, counting becomes possible.

Which endpoints can be joined?

After n steps, suppose u went up and v went down. Then u + v = n and u − v = b − a. These have whole-number answers only when n and b − a have the same parity, and only when n ≥ |b − a|. The applet quietly drops one step if the parity is wrong; this page does the same. With a = 3, b = 4, n = 9, the walk from A to B takes 9 steps.

Counting the routes

Once the walk is reachable, u = (n + b − a) / 2 steps go up and the rest go down. Any ordering of those up-steps gives a different route, so the number of walks is the binomial coefficient C(n, u). For the starting values that is C(9, 5) = 126. Press Ten walks a few times: the coloured paths are random samples from exactly that collection.

The reflection idea

Now ask how many walks from a positive height a ever touch or cross the axis. Take the part of such a walk before its first touch and reflect it in the axis; keep the rest as it was. You now have an ordinary walk from −a to b. This is a one-to-one match, so the number of touching walks equals the number of all walks from −a to b. That is the Reflection Lemma.

What was checked

The logic test counts walks two ways: by that binomial formula and by listing every up/down sequence for starts, ends and step counts up to 12. It also compares each generated walk, step by step, with a second transcription of the applet's choice rule, checks that every reachable walk arrives at B, and verifies the reflection correspondence for small positive heights. The applet's parity shortening and its option limits are checked too.

Set a = 1, b = 1 and n = 6, then send ten walks. How many different shapes can you spot?
